lines.caption: This is a tour of pull request 37, a weekly watcher that turns each new Thunar release into an issue and a pull request.
It has three parts: what this PR adds, how it was built and verified, and what comes later.
Part 1. What this PR adds.
Each week a cloud session runs check.sh, which finds the newest upstream tag that main doesn't have.
lines.say: Each week a cloud session runs the check script, which finds the newest upstream tag that main doesn't have.

lines.caption: If a release is already in flight, or you skipped this one, the session reports it and stops.
Otherwise it opens an issue for the release, with upstream's release notes.
It merges the release tag on the issue's own branch, keeping every fork change.
It writes the explainer page and narration that CI requires.
Then it pushes the branch and opens a pull request into main.
CI builds it and runs every verify script as a regression suite.
And you merge it, as with any other pull request.
Until now someone had to notice a new Xfce release and merge it by hand.
Main is upstream's 4.20.10 plus the fork's commits, so each release is one merge of its tag.
lines.say: Main is upstream's four point twenty point ten plus the fork's commits, so each release is one merge of its tag.

lines.caption: An open PR means waiting; an issue a failed run left behind is reported as stuck, for you to clear.
Conflicts are resolved file by file, then a file-list check confirms the fork's changes survived.
After installing, the split-view crash check stays a manual step for you.
Today the check prints none, because main already has the newest 4.20 release.
lines.say: Today the check prints none, because main already has the newest four point twenty release.

lines.caption: A newer stable series is reported but never merged, since it needs new Xfce libraries.
Development tags, with odd minor numbers, are ignored.
The PR adds the skill, its check script, and this explainer.
To pause the watcher, turn its task off; to skip a release, close its PR, and its issue as not planned.
Part 2. How it was built and verified.
It was checked against upstream's real tags and main's real history.
Against main, the check found nothing new.
Against a copy of main rebuilt on 4.20.9, it found 4.20.10.
lines.say: Against a copy of main rebuilt on four point twenty point nine, it found four point twenty point ten.

lines.caption: A fake newer series was reported, and an unreachable upstream gave an error.
Merging 4.20.10 into that copy by hand gave a tree identical to main.
lines.say: Merging four point twenty point ten into that copy by hand gave a tree identical to main.

lines.caption: A fake 4.20.11 release merged into main the same way, changing only two small files.
lines.say: A fake four point twenty point eleven release merged into main the same way, changing only two small files.

lines.caption: A full run that opens a real issue and PR was not run; that is the test after the merge.
A fresh review agent found four problems in the skill, all fixed, and one more was found while testing.
The biggest: a test must start from a rebuilt copy of main, not a plain upstream tag.
CI's own review found more in six rounds; the test now merges a small fake release instead of the whole fork.
The weekly schedule and the test PR can only run once this is merged.
Part 3. What comes later: the schedule and a test run.
After you merge, the weekly task is created and a test run merges a fake 4.20.11 release.
lines.say: After you merge, the weekly task is created and a test run merges a fake four point twenty point eleven release.

lines.caption: From then on, each new release arrives as an issue and a pull request.
In short: new Thunar releases now come to you as ready-to-check pull requests.
